segments.text: IGOR BABUSCHKIN: All right, folks.
So like I mentioned, the coding agents
have been tremendously successful.
Now, we're all wondering, what's the next big thing?
What is the next step?
And you've presented your personal directions for this.
So one feature that I think is pretty common among all
of the new directions that people are pursuing
is, it's getting harder and harder
to generate those rewards that we can use to power
reinforcement learning.
So I'm curious, how do you think about the difficulty of getting
rewards in your particular domain?
Do you think there are new techniques you
can use to get those rewards?
Or how do you think of this?
Starting with Ed, maybe.
ED CHI: Yeah.
The difficulty with rewards is really
because the predominant paradigm over the last couple of years
have been about using correctness as a feedback
to the RL process.
And the reward functions were pretty
easy to build when you have a correctness that's
built into the question that you're asking.
But there are many questions that we
want to ask, including in science,
as Richard was mentioning, that the answer may not
be correct or not correct, may be somewhere in between.
And the challenge in building those reward functions,
it's not just in figuring out some approximate solution
to that, but it's rather that the RL process is very, very
good at finding loopholes in the reward function
when it's not a black and white kind of answer.
So we call this reward hacking in the actual development
of the algorithms.
And we see it manifest in actually,
model instabilities when we have these more complicated reward
functions.
So to summarize, therefore, I think one way
to think about this whole RL thing
and using correctness function is, as I mentioned in my talk,
it's a little bit like teaching your kids, when it's wrong,
you just slap them on their butt,
and then you don't give them any more explanation why they were
wrong, other than just figure it out.
And so I think this bottom-up training process is actually,
sorry for saying it this way, but it's
a very dumb way of teaching.
I think, actually, what we're seeing with distillation
and SFT, coming back into vogue, what we're seeing
is actually, a lot more top-down processing in teaching,
where some people find it distasteful,
because it feels like we're using human brains to teach
machine brains, if you will, and it doesn't feel as emergent.
But that's what I believe is that we
need to have more top-down processing injected into the AI
training process.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Thank you.
Dogus, how are things looking with the furnace?
Is it a generating rewards?
EKIN DOGUS CUBUK: Yeah.
So there are two kinds of issues with furnaces.
So one of them is, as Ed mentioned,
you don't always know if the thing worked or not.
You take the thing out of the furnace.
It's actually obvious.
It might have partially worked.
And in fields where LLMs and RL has made a huge impact,
I think there are two specific things that really help.
One is, there is a very clear yes or no.
We just talked about this.
The other one is the, how much of the variables
are in the context?
So when you're programming, when you're
doing theoretical computer science,
math, all the contexts you might need
could be available to the LLM.
The problem with physics is, we have more atoms
than we can track.
And this is why thermodynamics was a big deal,
because in the 19th century, we realized,
instead of having to model 10 to the 23 atoms that make up a mole
of matter, you can just use a few variables, like pressure,
energy, volume, et cetera.
So we have to give up on providing
all the relevant context to the LLM,
because there is no way we can do that.
So then the question is, what can we provide?
And is it sufficient?
That's why it's really important to add
as much metrology characterization
as possible, maybe even more than before,
and just provide as much context as possible about what
happened in the furnace or in the thin film chamber
to the LLM.
RICHARD SOCHER: Yeah.
I think those are all really interesting.
I mentioned it in the UK machine.
You have human current knowledge.
You have scientific measurements.
Then you have simulations, which are hard at scale
with current computers.
And then you have to have real-life experiments.
And then hopefully, you can get some
of those inner loops resolved.
I think, in terms of reward functions,
there's also this whole idea that I've
been thinking about recently on metacognition.
I think if you truly have something that's
super intelligent, it wouldn't just robotically do
exactly what you asked it to.
There's, in some sense, no research
right now on subjective functions rather than
objective functions that we're all working on.
And so one way that these can emerge
is if you give AI the right environment that
is not as easily reward hackable,
which I think is the number one concern for safety.
Also, it's just alignment.
But I do have to say that I'm cautiously optimistic.
And I want to maybe invite folks to see Wispr Flow, which
is like a voice recognition app of sorts,
as a first sign of things to come as AI gets better.
Wispr Flow doesn't exactly write what you say,
it writes what you mean.
And most AI currently does very poorly,
exactly do what you say, like, make this benchmark number go
higher.
But you didn't mean like by hacking Hugging Face.
But I think, eventually, that will get resolved.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Cool.
So one thing I'm really curious about, because these agents,
they have this promise of accelerating us.
Are you actually seeing real world acceleration
from using your models?
So, Richard, how are things looking at at Recursive?
RICHARD SOCHER: It is nuts.
I really think we have a fairly small team,
but they act as if they're like an order of magnitude more
people.
It's much less about headcount these days
than it is about agent count.
And if you want to yield hundreds or even
several thousands of agents, you need a lot of compute.
And so I think the future in which
a lot of these forward-leaning organizations
actually spend more on compute than on headcount,
and people is not.
It's very likely to happen, especially at the frontier.
And yeah, I would love to hear from you, actually, also
on, how much robotic process automation can you do now?
And is the bottleneck the intelligence or actually
just the mechanics?
EKIN DOGUS CUBUK: I mean, for the experimental side,
I feel like the biggest bottleneck is characterization
and analysis, because it's not too hard to just mix things
and then try 1,000 things at the same time.
But what's really hard is to understand what you actually
made.
And this is actually really good news,
because AI can do really well at this.
You can show AI how to do, for example, XRD refinement,
how to use Rietveld refinement tools, use
simulations in the loop.
And it's like, doing characterization analysis well
isn't as hard as discovering something new,
it's just like using the tools correctly.
And I think this is great news for science,
because now, we can try many more things
and intelligently analyze them before.
Of course, we do a lot of coding.
The theoretical physicists do coding.
The experimentalists do coding.
And LLMs have completely revolutionized that, of course.
Also on the simulation side, so force fields
are these things that people have
used for more than a century to approximate quantum mechanics.
I think one could argue that even Einstein's first paper was
a force field paper.
And in the last 10 years, because
of graph neural networks, force fields changed permanently.
And it's amazing now how much of the periodic table
we can model without even doing quantum chemistry.
So yeah, really exciting on the capabilities side.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Are people at Google using agents
to accelerate themselves?
ED CHI: Yeah, we're obviously using agents in our coding work.
But I think, as Richard and Dogus were just describing,
I was realizing that maybe, I think
about the problem a little bit from a weird way, if you will.
The reality is that I think about, is
that there has been a decent amount of tension that's
happened ever since the beginning of the chain
of thought era, is that agent harnesses is really
the evolution of prompt engineering today,
because people started with prompts.
And then they figured out that they
can put more things in the prompt
to get the model to do what they wanted it to do.
Then they realized, they should programmably
put these prompts together.
Then they figured out things like link chain
to figure out how to chain prompts together,
so to get it to do more complex tasks.
Then they realized, they can just
put a whole program around the generation of the prompt,
and how many prompts, and how to chain them together.
And then that evolved into agent harnesses and coding harnesses.
So that whole evolution, of course, all of us
have been in the field and have been watching that going.
But the tension that is inherent in your question
is, there have been, for three or four
years, this debate about, how much should be in the model?
And how much should be in the programmable framework,
the agent harness that we call it now?
We used to just call it programmable LLM frameworks.
And in fact, I'm sure in the audience today,
there are people who are trying out different agent harnesses
with different models.
And they're realizing that they're
evaluating all pairs of these relationships.
They're using a strong, very structured agent harness,
working with a very weak model.
And then when they have a very strong model,
they try to put less harness around it.
By the way, it's just very interesting to me that we use
the word "harness."
The word "harness" obviously comes from horses.
The reason why we're called engines horsepower
is because the Industrial Revolution, with engines,
we all became engineers.
We're supposed to work on engines,
like tightening screws and stuff like that.
And then the engine mount is basically the harness.
So the reality is the prompt engineering
and the harness is the structure that's
trying to get the engine to do what we want it to do.
So there's this tension between the harness and the model
capability.
And people are realizing, when you have a strong model,
you should use a weaker prompting technique and weaker
programmable harnesses.
But when you have a weaker model,
you could mitigate its capabilities
using a stronger harness, a more structured.
But however, I think people are also coming to the realization
when they do this, that the two together
can only reach a particular performance level.
And there is a plateau that we can't seem to go over
at the current moment.
And that is actually the major bottleneck or barrier
currently facing the industry in my opinion.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: That's the frontier.
That's literally the frontier right now.
RICHARD SOCHER: Actually, maybe jamming on that,
I do think the whole field of AI is stuck below what
I call Anthropic bounds, not just the company,
but this idea that we measure models in terms of Elo scores
of which human said this model is better than that model.
We measure a lot of our benchmarks based
on how many of the human-designed labels
and human-designed classes and tasks
did you get right in this subset of images, and reasoning
questions, and so on?
All of those have implicit and sometimes, very explicit
human bounds.
You can get 100 out of 100% of the questions right,
then that's the maximum you can get to.
And yeah, maybe humans get 95, and you
get 5% above the human baseline, but that's it.
Where do you go from there?
The only way to get out of that is
through simulations and some verifiers, where you can then
get superhuman capabilities or in these open-ended evolutionary
environments.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Well, now, I have a really, really tough
question.
So let's see if one of you can find an answer here,
but get ready for this one.
So we're all at the frontier.
And at the frontier, you need access
to tremendous compute resources.
You've got colleagues that are experts in their field.
But there are so many people in academia
and especially, PhD students out there who don't get access
to those resources today, but they still
want to contribute to the frontier,
they want to contribute to agents and the future of agents.
Do you have any tips for those folks?
What are the directions?
What are the ideas that they should focus on,
where there's a potential to have big impact with fewer
resources and contribute to these frontier efforts?
Anyone, is something that comes to mind?
RICHARD SOCHER: I think there's a ton of opportunity, still, .
There's so many underexplored areas and application areas
of AI too.
Sure.
Maybe the research area of pretraining,
and mid and post-scenario training,
it's not the best one for PhD students at a university.
But I had this paper in 2018, on a two-level reinforcement
learning setup called the AI economist,
where you essentially had agents that just optimized
their own utility functions, and you can make assumptions
based on, how many hours would people want to work?
And some people are willing to work 100-hour workweeks.
And some people only want to work 10-hour workweeks.
And then they're unmotivated.
And so long story short, you can then
have this simulation of agents that are economic agents trying
to optimize their own utility, collect resources, block others,
build monopolies, whatever.
And then you had an AI economist that
would set taxes and subsidies, and basically,
could now simulate billions and billions
of years of taxation and subsidization,
essentially, political philosophy,
and try to find the best way to set these taxation
schemes, and tax brackets, and so on, based on a goal
that you gave it, like productivity multiplied
with equality, or sustainability,
or whatever you politically care about, middle class, whatever
politicians say.
Now, what's interesting is that paper never had its GPT moment,
where someone actually took that idea and massively scaled it up.
And so the whole field of economics
is still like pre-AI era.
When you look at economists, there's
one really famous economist from Berkeley, actually, Saez.
He invented this famous Saez formula.
And it's provably correct in a one step economy,
where there is no adaptation, there's
no adjustment or no temporal sequences, and so on.
That's the state of the field of economics.
And if you now realize that AI could do so much more there,
and you can simulate people better and better,
especially in the aggregate statistics, you can realize,
there's so much low-hanging fruit
for PhD students to take AI and apply it to economics.
And that is just one of many examples.
There are still so many other fields
that you can research in and then
combine I with that are extremely underexplored.
And I'm excited that venture capital is now excited also
about chemistry and some more physics, and obviously, biology,
but there also is still so much low-hanging fruit
to apply to these various scientific fields.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Any more ideas for the--
EKIN DOGUS CUBUK: Yeah, I would say, I mean,
so it's hard to predict the future.
In four years, if these robots are
as dexterous and intelligent, creative,
has a sense of style as humans, I
think this answer gets very complicated.
But today, I think it's very easy to say,
robots are not as dexterous, they're not as creative,
they don't really have a sense of interestingness.
And in that case, I think what the students should study,
in my opinion, is the fundamentals.
So for example, today, very practically,
if somebody, as a scientist, applies to Periodic Labs, to me,
it doesn't make too much of a difference
if they've been using agentic tools to run simulations,
because there's something you can probably
learn how to do pretty quickly.
The thing that's very unique, and unfortunately,
getting more and more rare, is just
people who understand the fundamentals
about the physics you're studying
or the experiments you're studying.
I mean, I used to joke, but when I was at Google,
we used to have these interns coming in.
And I used to hire interns from physics labs,
to do physics research, and they'd
be so much stronger on the machine learning
than the physics.
And maybe I'm just being too uncreative here,
because back then, I used to worry that, as you know,
all the simulation tools are in Fortran, and C, and C++,
and all the kids are only doing Python.
I was like, oh, are we screwed?
What's going to happen in the future?
But I think that's resolved now.
Now, even though we don't have it yet,
we can see that these agents will
be able to give us Python code or JAX code, given a Fortran
package.
Great.
But there's still a lot of things that these machines
cannot do, like being creative about the fundamentals,
coming up with a true innovation on our understanding
of the universe, being able to run experiments,
coming up with new experiments.
So at least from my selfish perspective,
I really feel like the big alpha today
is understanding the fundamentals of the application.
And then you can connect it with machine learning.
ED CHI: When I was working at Google Brain-- when
Dogus and I were both in Google Brain,
before the chain of thought era, I
remember Danny Zhao came to me.
And he said, all these people in Google Brain,
with control over the resources, makes it very difficult
for me to do research.
So the same complaint in a way that you're
inherent in the question that you're asking.
He said to me, how do I deal with this problem?
I said, I don't know.
Go think about how humans think.
And maybe we can figure out a way
to inject these processes into the model.
And what I'm about to tell you, I hope,
doesn't get me fired from Google, by the way.
One day, he came to me, and he said,
I want to do a bunch of experiment on GPT.
Is that allowed?
And it's like, because we're at Google, we should be using PaLM.
That was our model.
So we should be using PaLM.
And I was like, I can't get my hands on chips to do
all these experiments on PaLM.
I don't have access to the checkpoints, blah, blah, blah,
blah blah.
And he said, can I just use GPT?
Who will pay for it?
And I pulled out my credit card, and I said, here's
my credit card.
So he charged all these APIs usage.
This is before ChatGPT.
So this is no free resources.
You actually have to buy API key and all that.
He racked up a couple thousand dollars worth of charges
or something like that.
And then we wrote the paper.
That became a chain of thought.
So even then, Google was spending billions of dollars
already to train these large language models.
And here comes a new idea that was top-down
rather than bottom-up, not thinking
about next token prediction, but rather,
thinking about next idea prediction.
And I think we ultimately spent less than $10,000 to come up
with the next idea.
Now, you might say, oh, wow, that
was three or four years ago.
I think the paper was January-ish of '22, '21.
And so you say, oh, wow, that's not possible in 2026.
Well, where were you when Peter Steinberger
was working on OpenClaw?
I would argue, a lot of people really
started to pay attention to agentic programming framework
when he really put all these technologies together.
And that didn't cost billions of dollars.
He was just some dude.
I think he presented yesterday.
I was flying in from Taiwan last night,
and so I didn't get to attend his talk.
But I mean, here's a guy who's just like, oh,
I'm going to experiment with agentic frameworks.
And then he came up with some new thing about how
to think about the problem.
So I think the state that we're in,
when academia are complaining about this,
it's a little bit like there are many mature fields that
have moved like this.
Like experimental physics, at some point,
people are going to complain, I don't have access
to a linear accelerator.
Or when I was working on supercomputing back
in the '90s, I didn't have access to a Cray Y-MP.
So therefore, I don't have 2.6 gigaflops
or whatever it is to do.
By the way, does anyone know why we were investing
in supercomputer in 1990?
Does anyone know?
Anyone can raise their-- yeah, what's the reason?
AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]
ED CHI: What kind of simulations?
AUDIENCE: Nuclear.
ED CHI: That's right, nuclear simulations.
It was because of the nuclear ban treaty.
We wanted to simulate real physical processes,
so we built supercomputers.
That was the reason.
That came from a complaint about the fact
that we can't blow things up anymore.
So we're going to have to come up
with a new way of understanding physics,
and that was supercomputers.
So we're very good at coming up with new ways of looking
at old problems as well as new problems.
And so I think computer science as a field or AI
as a field needs to continue to look at this.
When everybody is working on RL, you should be thinking,
what's the next idea?
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Yeah, right.
RICHARD SOCHER: It's interesting.
You touch on an interesting point, which
is like, I still remember in 2010, when I submitted
my first neural nets for NLP papers, they got this rejected.
People are like, we don't do neural nets in NLP conferences.
They didn't even look at the experiments.
And even when we submitted the paper for prompt engineering,
where we had one neural network to answer
any and all kinds of questions, the reviewers literally said,
that makes no sense.
You should never have one model to try to answer
different kinds of questions.
They should all be different models.
And it was unfathomable for them.
And they rejected that paper too.
It's all public on OpenReview and that ICLR submission
on Decca NLP.
The paper eventually got cited five times
by the first GPT paper.
And it had its run now.
But there's now almost like a monoculture that
is similar to the monoculture from 2010
when it's all anti-neural nets.
And now, it's almost all only neural nets.
So I think it'll be good to start thinking again
about completely different approaches.
Not everything is a transformer.
Transformer is just one sample in a very large
equivalence class.
And I think there are other better classes of algorithms
still to be explored.
I think, compute substrates, obviously, we can do better.
We know the brain has more flops per watt than any
of the hardware we have.
So there's so much research there
still to be done and so on.
I feel like, there's no excuse for researchers in AI
and outside of AI, not to still do academic work.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Yeah.
That's a good lesson in resilience
there for PhD students as well.
Just because your paper gets rejected,
it could still be the next big breakthrough.
Nobody really knows the future.
So yeah, a lot of folks in the field
tell me similar stories about their big breakthroughs.
One thing I would add is, while the research at the frontier
is getting more and more expensive and challenging,
at the same time, we're also seeing
some of the tools being more and more democratized.
So I'm thinking especially of open weight models, for example.
So if you wanted to start off with a really capable LLM
or really capable agent, you can actually
take a powerful open weight model today,
and then do a lot of interesting research and development
on top of that.
And even the tools for post-training and reinforcement
learning are getting democratized.
I mentioned the River AI API earlier.
And tkinter is another example of these kinds
of tools, where even with a very limited budget,
you can do really, really interesting work.
So I think this is also a big opportunity for researchers
to be able to do really, actually
frontier work without a huge cost attached to it.
So we're getting to the end of the session,
so I wanted to go to the big closing statement.
And so I wanted to ask you folks,
let's make a prediction for the next 12 months.
We've seen, this year was the year
of coding agents and the incredible economic success that
came with them.
Over the next 12 months, what will be the next big agent
breakthrough?
Where do you see the big impact in the world and economic impact
as well?
So maybe starting with Ed.
ED CHI: Well, as many of you know,
if you especially attended last year's summit,
I was making a prediction that personalization
was going to be really big.
And I know Richard has also worked on personalization
as well.
It's been very surprising how slow it has been,
to be perfectly honest.
But I think a lot of the issue has
been around data and the sparsity of data
for personalization in the consumer space.
My prediction in the next 12 months or so
would be that, usually, it takes three tries for these things
to succeed.
And I think there will be a good try, probably,
within the next 12 months or so in this space.
And most of the issues will be centered
around two things-- one is data that I mentioned,
the integration.
The other is actually having to do
with being able to really make good inductive inferences
and reasoning.
Because so much of the model these days
are very focused around deductive reasoning.
You bought this, therefore, I think
you were going to buy this next.
You bought a bicycle, so you're going to need tires or something
like that.
There's a reasoning chain that's very deductive like that.
But actually, a lot of the recommendation tasks,
the personalization tasks are very ambiguous.
And they need more induction.
if you bought a turntable, we can
infer that maybe you like classical music, for example,
or jazz.
I'm a big vinyl collector.
So by the way, one of the reason I came up to Berkeley
is because Rasputin is not far away from here,
so I could walk over and peruse the aisles there.
But that's an example of induction.
Google Maps should be recommending, hey, by the way,
it's Rasputin.
It's less than a five-minute walk from here.
You should go check it out.
So that's the kind of inductive reasoning,
I think in the future, in the personalization space,
we're going to see within the next 12 months.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Yeah, Dogus.
EKIN DOGUS CUBUK: Yeah.
So speaking of induction, I think
if you look at what happened so far in terms
of how LLMs and agents did something incredibly different
in the sciences and math, I think
it's easy to say that it's been in math, theoretical computer
science, and programming.
So if you were to do induction, the next step
should be fields where pure theory goes a long way.
So maybe this will be your expertise
with the particle theory.
Or maybe it'll be in astrophysics, I'm not sure.
It could also be computational physics,
where there's some really difficult problems
in computational physics.
That's not necessarily the real universe,
but still very important on its own right.
So it could be that as well.
I don't know if it's going to be in 12 months.
Again, it's really hard to predict the future,
but it does suggest that, given the current trend,
that could be the next step.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: It feels like there's
a lot of results in mathematics coming out every day now,
so getting more and more theorems proven.
So I think that's a very promising bet.
Richard.
RICHARD SOCHER: Man, it's going to be an exciting 12 months.
Maybe I'll cheat by doing three.
I think, number 1, we'll see more proactive consumer
interfaces to these models that capture
more and more of your context, and hence,
will predict recommendations before you ask for them.
There are already a few startups that
are growing a little bit here and there,
but I think more of that is to come.
I think in biology, we're going to see the first and much faster
clinical trials and getting more and more drugs and proteins
developed with AI that are then succeeding
at a higher rate than currently as they get into later stage
trials.
And then we're going to have the first baby forms
of recursive self-improvement.
And I'm cheating there, because the best predictions are those
that you're going to work on yourself
and try to make them true.
So I think it's feasible, it's happening.
We're very confident.
And it's then, of course, a question of,
well, but how much compute do you give it?
And how hard are the tasks that you give it to work on,
and the environments, and all of that?
So sometimes, people think that there's
going to be this hard takeoff scenario.
And despite being extremely excited and optimistic about AI,
the hard takeoff scenario, where everyone
loses their jobs or the AI kills everyone, all of these
are highly unrealistic sci-fi.
And so I also predict in the negative
that none of the doomsday scenarios
will happen at all, whatsoever.
And just like GPT was too dangerous to release
to the world, there will be no open source
model that would be too dangerous to release
to the world.
IGOR BABUSCHKIN: Thank you so much.
And I hope you all enjoyed this little glimpse at the frontier.
[APPLAUSE]
So let's thank the speakers.
Thank you.
